design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; PROSPERO CRD42019126994, registered 28 February 2019, the day of the search) of human experimental studies that gave the same dose of THC by the same route with and without cannabidiol (CBD) and had a placebo or pre-drug baseline condition. Four databases searched on 28 February 2019, English-language peer-reviewed reports only. 23 articles reporting 16 studies (13 crossover, 3 parallel-group; 466 healthy volunteers in all), published 1974 to 2019. Table 1 lists the two experiments of Dalton et al. (1976) as separate studies, and groups several articles from one sample (for example Nadulski et al., 2005, with Juckel et al., 2007, Roser et al., 2008 and 2009, and Stadelmann et al., 2011). Narrative synthesis by outcome domain because outcomes were too heterogeneous to pool. Risk of bias rated with a Cochrane tool by two reviewers; Table 1 shows only an overall rating per study (domain judgments are in Appendix G, not in the file). Read as the journal pre-proof.
can_establish: What the published, English-language laboratory studies up to early 2019 reported when CBD was given with, or shortly before, a matched dose of THC to healthy volunteers, outcome by outcome, and how consistent those reports were across very different doses, routes, timings and THC:CBD ratios.
cannot_establish: How large any effect of CBD on THC's acute effects is (nothing was pooled and effect sizes are rarely given); whether it depends on dose, ratio or route (the authors found no consistent pattern, and the conditions tested rarely match each other); whether findings apply to people with psychiatric vulnerability, frequent use or past bad reactions (all participants were screened healthy volunteers, mostly with occasional use, and two studies included people who had never used cannabis); or whether the literature is free of reporting bias (no assessment beyond an informal statement).

sample.recruitment: Database search (MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL Plus) on 28 February 2019 using terms for THC and CBD only, with Ovid filters for human studies and English, plus additional sources; four articles published after the search were added (pp. 10–12 of the journal pre-proof). Participants in the included studies were healthy volunteers in the UK, USA, Australia, Brazil and Germany (Table 1, pp. 65–71).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: a condition or group given acute THC; a matched condition or group given the same THC dose by the same route together with CBD under experimental conditions; a placebo condition or a no-drug pre-drug baseline; peer-reviewed; English. Excluded: conference abstracts, theses, reviews, supplements, letters and other non-peer-reviewed material; studies without a matched THC dose and route; repeated-dosing studies; studies whose analysis did not compare THC alone with THC plus CBD (or each with placebo); non-human studies (2.2, pp. 9–10).
sample.demographics: All 16 studies used healthy volunteers (3.2, p. 15). Samples ranged from 4 to 155 participants; one parallel study and five crossover studies had 4 to 8 participants per treatment cell (pp. 13–14). All but two studies required previous cannabis use; Table 1 shows that 18 of 40 participants in Karniol et al. (1974) and 3 of 8 in Zuardi et al. (1982) had never used cannabis, and that most other samples had used occasionally (for example at least once but never regularly, or at most 2 to 3 times a week); one study recruited 24 people using cannabis daily and 24 using it recreationally (Hindocha et al., 2015, with Morgan et al., 2018). Five studies enrolled men only (Dalton, Guy and Robson, Hollister and Gillespie, Hunt, Karniol). Ages in Table 1 run from 18 to 70.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Table 1 records study-level losses, for example three of 14 not completing in Arkell et al. (2019), one of them discharged because of raised blood pressure and heart rate; failed cannulation in three of 48 in Englund et al. (2013); 19 further people withdrawn or excluded in Haney et al. (2016); 20 to 24 of 28 analysed in Nadulski et al. (2005), where three women had a panic attack (pp. 65, 67, 68, 70, 72).
sample.selection_effects: English-language, peer-reviewed reports only; no trial registries or grey literature. All participants were screened healthy volunteers, so people with psychiatric vulnerability, frequent heavy use or previous bad reactions are largely absent; the authors note that studies may have excluded people at risk of adverse effects (4.3, p. 34). Two of the 16 studies (six of the 23 articles) were co-authored by review authors.

exposure.measurement: Experimental administration in each included study, as listed in Table 1 (pp. 65–71). By the editors' count from Table 1, THC was given orally in 5 studies, intravenously in 3, smoked in 3, vaporised in 3 and by oromucosal spray in 2; CBD was given at the same time as THC or as a pre-treatment (five studies, from 480 minutes to 5 minutes before THC). The review's own count of routes and dose ranges (3.3, p. 15) differs from Table 1 (see reporting issues).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as printed in Table 1 and the text: THC 1.25 to 2 mg intravenously; 8 to 13.75 mg vaporised; about 42 mg or 0.025 mg/kg smoked; 10 to 30 mg, 0.215 mg/kg or 0.5 mg/kg orally; 10 to 15 mg by oromucosal spray. CBD from 5 mg intravenously to 1500 mg orally in three divided doses (Hunt et al., 1981), with THC:CBD ratios varying widely between studies. Single sessions; repeated dosing was excluded by design.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed at review level. Abstinence rules before sessions differed between studies (Table 1); the review names participants' own cannabis use outside the study as a possible source of residual effects (3.5, p. 16). In Arkell et al. (2019) the THC-alone condition contained less than 1.25 mg CBD and the placebo less than 1.25 mg THC and CBD (Table 1, p. 65).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Varied by study (Table 1): not reported in Dalton et al. (1976) and Hollister and Gillespie (1975); 12 hours without cannabis, alcohol or tobacco in Haney et al. (2016); 24 hours without alcohol or illicit drugs in the two UCL studies; 48 hours on site in Hunt et al. (1981); 15 days in Zuardi et al. (1982); 30 days or one month in Guy and Robson (2003), Nicholson et al. (2004) and Nadulski et al. (2005); urine or oral-fluid screens in several.

comparison.controls: Within each study, the same THC dose by the same route without CBD (or after placebo pre-treatment), and a placebo condition or a pre-drug baseline. The five pre-treatment designs had no pure placebo condition and used baseline measures instead (3.3, p. 15).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. 13 within-person crossover studies and 3 randomized parallel-group studies (Karniol et al., 1974: groups balanced for age and weight).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense (experimental comparisons). Participant characteristics the authors say can change THC's acute effects (cannabis history, potency and frequency of use, psychosis-proneness, sex, genetic factors) were not assessed in most studies (4, 2nd paragraph, pp. 31–32).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants in the crossover designs; abstinence rules varied between studies (see exposure).

outcomes.instruments: As used by the primary studies (Table 1; section 3.6): plasma THC and metabolites; pulse and blood pressure; visual analogue scales of intoxication, the ARCI-Ma and a modified Cornell Medical Index; anxiety ratings and the STAI, and the graded symptom scale of Karniol and Carlini; PANSS, BPRS, Psychotomimetic States Inventory and State Social Paranoia Scale; memory and attention tasks (HVLT-R, prose recall, N-back, digit span, DSST, divided attention, PASAT, time production, verbal fluency); auditory event-related potentials (mismatch negativity, P300); emotion-recognition and effort-for-reward tasks; fMRI; psychomotor and simulated-driving tasks; sleep measures.
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study risk of bias was rated by two reviewers with a Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, named as RoB 2 but cited to the 2011 tool (2.6, p. 12) and to Higgins et al. (2016) in the limitations (p. 37); only one overall rating per study is shown (Table 1).
outcomes.operationalization: An influence of CBD was any reported difference between THC alone and THC with CBD on any outcome; the review planned to report all such comparisons (2.8, p. 12). Table 1 codes each finding as CBD increasing, decreasing or not changing THC's effect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable at review level: no statistical tests were run; ten outcome domains are synthesized narratively (3.6.1 to 3.6.10). The authors note that not all primary studies corrected for multiple analyses (4.7, p. 38).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles and abstracts, and then full texts, were each screened independently by two reviewers with a third for disagreements; two reviewers extracted data, a third resolved discrepancies and checked a random subset (2.4, 2.5, p. 11).

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled; the synthesis is narrative because heterogeneity of outcomes precluded meta-analysis (3.6, p. 17). No standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported. The text gives counts of studies, sample sizes and a few raw values, for example a mean fall in systolic blood pressure at 3 hours of 10.3 mmHg after THC 10 mg alone, 4.4 mmHg with CBD 10 mg and 5.1 mmHg after placebo (Guy and Robson, 2003; p. 20); Grade 4 effects in 4 of 5 participants after oral THC 30 mg alone and in 3 of 15 when oral CBD 15 to 60 mg was added (Karniol et al., 1974; p. 22); THC clearance of 17 and 20.9 ml/min/kg without and with CBD in 4 participants (Hunt et al., 1981; p. 18).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42019126994, registered 28 February 2019, the date of the search (2.1, p. 9); PRISMA checklist in Appendix A and protocol in Appendix B, neither in the file. Whether the protocol specified the narrative synthesis, and whether there were deviations, cannot be checked from the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review reports every comparison of THC with and without CBD it found, by its stated inclusive approach; nothing is pooled. Several counts and study descriptions in the text disagree with Table 1 (see reporting issues). The informal judgment of publication bias (3.5, p. 16) is not an assessment.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level. The authors note that six studies had 4 to 8 participants per treatment cell and that some studies may have been underpowered (pp. 13–14, 38).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 16 small laboratory studies of healthy volunteers (466 people in all; six studies with 4 to 8 per cell), CBD given with or before a matched THC dose mostly did not change THC's pharmacokinetics, heart rate, subjective intoxication (seven of nine studies found no difference) or psychomotor and driving impairment. Lower anxiety or psychosis-like effects with CBD were reported in three studies: oral THC 30 mg in groups of 5 (Karniol et al., 1974; Grade 4 effects in 4 of 5 versus 3 of 15, no test reported in the review), intravenous THC 1.25 mg in 6 people (Bhattacharyya et al., 2010), and intravenous THC 1.5 mg in a 48-person parallel trial in which the mean PANSS increase did not differ but fewer people given CBD had a clinically significant rise (Englund et al., 2013); Zuardi et al. (1982; n=8) also found a smaller STAI rise. With inhaled cannabis, Morgan et al. (2018; n=48) found no difference in psychotomimetic effects, and Arkell et al. (2019; n=14) found anxiety raised in both conditions at 15 minutes and still raised only without CBD at one hour. One study found higher peak plasma THC with CBD (Arkell et al., 2019). Results on memory, attention and emotion processing went both ways.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion are hedged (findings mixed; some evidence that CBD may reduce some effects; no dose-response). Gaps: (1) the discussion says three studies showed “significantly fewer participants” with extreme anxiety and psychotic-like effects (4.3, p. 33), but for two of them the review gives only counts in groups of 5 and 6 without a test, and the third found no difference in the mean; (2) the highlights and discussion call the risk of bias “typically low” (pp. 2, 31), while the limitations list inadequately described randomisation, allocation blinding and unexamined order effects (pp. 37–38), and Table 1 rates as low risk a pseudo-randomised study (Bhattacharyya et al., 2010) and one in which randomisation is not indicated (Nicholson et al., 2004); (3) the highlights say CBD did not alter subjective intoxication, while two of nine studies reported a reduction; (4) the harm-reduction section links these single-dose laboratory findings to consumer education and regulation (4.6, pp. 36–37) without any dose-response or route-specific result to support it.

timeline.event: Karniol et al.: oral CBD with oral THC 30 mg in parallel groups of 5; described in the review as the first report that CBD blocks THC's anxiety-provoking effects (included).
Bhattacharyya et al.: intravenous CBD before intravenous THC in 6 volunteers (included).
Englund et al.: oral CBD 600 mg before intravenous THC 1.5 mg, 48-person parallel trial (included).
Morgan et al.: vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg in 48 people; no difference in psychotomimetic effects and none by frequency of use or trait schizotypy (included).
Arkell et al.: vaporised cannabis with THC 13.75 mg, with and without CBD 13.75 mg, in 14 people; added after the search (included).
This review: the first systematic review of the question by the authors' account; narrative synthesis, nothing pooled.
Same first author and group: pooled analysis of four of the group's own crossover studies of THC versus placebo (CBD conditions not analysed), on frequency of use and schizotypy as moderators.
Zamarripa et al.: randomized clinical trial of oral THC co-administered with CBD on THC pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in healthy adults (to be appraised from the full text).
Chester et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of whether co-administered CBD changes plasma THC and its active metabolite (on the reading list; to be appraised from the full text).

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review of the question at the time and the one usually cited, but it pooled nothing, its three positive studies on anxiety and psychosis-like effects are small and mostly used oral or intravenous THC, and its pre-proof text and table disagree in several places. Later randomized studies of THC with and without CBD on the encyclopedia's reading list (Arkell et al., 2020, driving; Lawn et al., 2023, adults and adolescents; Zamarripa et al., 2023, oral THC) and the 2026 meta-analysis of CBD and plasma THC (Chester et al., 2026) should be read before any claim that CBD does or does not change THC's acute effects.

funding.funder: No specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (p. 38 of the journal pre-proof).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit and the Centre for Outcomes, Research and Effectiveness, University College London; University of Bath; King's College London (p. 1). Review authors T. P. Freeman, C. Hindocha, H. V. Curran and C. Mokrysz are co-authors of six of the 23 included articles (Hindocha et al., 2015 and 2019; Morgan et al., 2018; Lawn et al., 2016; T. P. Freeman et al., 2018; Wall et al., 2019; reference list), from two of the 16 studies, both rated at low risk of bias; C. Hindocha was the third reviewer for extraction and risk-of-bias disagreements (p. 11). This is not declared as a conflict. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, adequately powered randomized crossover trial in people who use cannabis regularly, comparing inhaled THC alone, THC with two or more CBD doses and placebo under identical routes and timing, with plasma THC measured and prespecified outcomes (anxiety, psychotomimetic states, memory, intoxication); or an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of the existing crossover trials.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Humans given acute THC; THC with CBD versus a matched THC dose and route; placebo or baseline control; all acute outcomes (2.2, 2.8).

PROSPERO CRD42019126994 registered on the day of the search (p. 9); the protocol (Appendix B) is not in the file, so whether it specified the synthesis plan and whether there were deviations cannot be checked.
Inclusion of acute experimental studies with a matched THC dose and route and a placebo or baseline control is justified, as is the exclusion of repeated dosing (pp. 9–10, 37).

Four relevant databases with a sensitive intervention-only strategy (Appendix C, not read) and a search within months of acceptance; but English-language and peer-reviewed-only restrictions without justification (English acknowledged only as a limitation, p. 16), grey literature excluded by design, no trial registries, and no reference-list searching reported.
Titles and abstracts, then full texts, screened independently by two reviewers, a third resolving disagreements (2.4, p. 11).
Two reviewers extracted data; discrepancies resolved with a third, who also checked a random subset (2.5, p. 11).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: a table of excluded studies is said to be in Appendix E and the flow diagram with reasons in Appendix F (p. 13); neither is in the file read, so whether each full-text exclusion is listed with a reason cannot be checked.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, aims, participants (number, sex, age, cannabis experience, abstinence rules), design, conditions with doses, routes and pre-treatment timing, outcomes, findings and risk of bias; the timing of outcome measurement is mostly absent, and several entries contradict the text (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A Cochrane risk-of-bias tool applied independently by two reviewers, but the version is unclear (RoB 2 named, 2011 tool cited), only an overall rating per study is shown (domains in Appendix G, not read), and two low ratings sit awkwardly with the tool: pseudo-randomisation (Bhattacharyya et al., 2010) and randomisation not indicated (Nicholson et al., 2004).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Only two industry-funded studies are named (Guy and Robson, 2003; Nicholson et al., 2004; p. 16); funding of the others is not reported.
Narrative synthesis; meta-analysis judged precluded by heterogeneity of outcomes (p. 17).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Each results subsection names the studies with some concerns, but the discussion and conclusions do not weigh them: the anxiety conclusion rests on three studies, two rated some concerns or unclear (Karniol et al., 1974; Zuardi et al., 1982), and the discussion calls risk of bias typically low. A close call.

Doses, routes, THC:CBD ratios, low oral CBD bioavailability, small samples and participant factors (cannabis history, psychosis-proneness, sex, genetics) are discussed as reasons for inconsistent findings (pp. 31–32).

No quantitative synthesis. The review nonetheless asserts a low risk of publication bias because many studies reported a mix of significant and non-significant findings (p. 16), which is not a method of detecting it.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No specific funding and no interests declared (p. 38); the review does not flag that four authors co-wrote six included articles.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can only be judged from Appendix E, which was not read; the overall rating does not depend on it. AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence because two critical items are not met: the search was restricted to English-language peer-reviewed reports without justification (item 4), and risk of bias was not weighed in the interpretation (item 13, a close call; if it were judged met, the rating would be low confidence). Items 2 and 9 are only partly met. This rates how far the review's summary can be trusted, not its usefulness: it is registered, transparent about its narrative approach, and its Table 1 is a usable map of the 16 studies. It may be cited for what each included study reported, with the study named, and for the absence of a consistent effect of CBD on THC's subjective intoxication, heart rate and pharmacokinetics in these laboratory studies; it should not be cited on its own for a general claim that CBD protects against THC-induced anxiety or psychosis-like effects.

key_findings.finding: The search on 28 February 2019 found 1808 records; 601 duplicates were removed and four articles published after the search were added; 1211 titles and abstracts were screened and 47 full texts assessed; 23 articles reporting 16 studies were included.

All 16 studies were human laboratory experiments; three used parallel groups and the rest crossover designs. Sample sizes ranged from 4 to 155, with 466 participants in total; one parallel and five crossover studies had 4 to 8 participants per treatment cell, and two studies were designed for safety and pharmacokinetics and were not powered to detect effects.
key_findings.note: The text names the third parallel study as Karniol and Carlini (1974), a different reference in the list; Table 1 and the rest of the text use Karniol et al. (1974). The total of 466 is reproduced from Table 1 if Bird et al. (1980) counts 155 and the Nadulski study 24 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: All studies enrolled healthy volunteers, and all but two (Karniol et al., 1974; Zuardi et al., 1982) included only people with previous cannabis use. Table 1 shows 18 of 40 participants in Karniol et al. (1974) and 3 of 8 in Zuardi et al. (1982) had never used cannabis, and one study recruited 24 people using cannabis daily and 24 using it recreationally.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Participants (p. 15); Table 1, Participants column (Hindocha et al., 2015, row on p. 68; Karniol et al., 1974, row on p. 69; Zuardi et al., 1982, row on p. 71)

key_findings.finding: Ten studies were rated at low risk of bias and six at some concerns; none at high risk. The domain-level table is in Appendix G (not in the file); Table 1 gives one overall rating per study, with both Dalton et al. (1976) experiments rated low, which completes the ten (the text names nine).
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Risk of bias within studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1, Risk of Bias column (pp. 65–71)

key_findings.finding: The review judged the risk of publication bias low because many studies reported a mixture of significant and non-significant findings, and named as further across-study biases the English-language restriction, industry funding of two studies (Guy and Robson, 2003; Nicholson et al., 2004), residual effects of participants' own cannabis use, and recognition of the placebo condition.
key_findings.locator: 3.5 Risk of bias across studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Eight studies measured pharmacokinetics; most found that CBD did not significantly change THC's pharmacokinetic profile. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): peak plasma THC was significantly higher after vaporised THC 13.75 mg with CBD 13.75 mg than after THC alone (area under the curve over 0–3 hours higher but not significantly). Nadulski et al. (2005; n=24): oral CBD 5.4 mg partly inhibited the hydroxylation of oral THC 10 mg, with wide variability. Guy and Robson (2003; n=24): later time to peak THC with CBD 10 mg (oromucosal spray). Hunt et al. (1981; n=4): 1500 mg oral CBD in three doses before intravenous THC 2 mg had no significant effect (clearance 17 versus 20.9 ml/min/kg). No significant differences in Bhattacharyya et al. (2010; n=6) or Englund et al. (2013; n=36).

Ten studies measured pulse: eight found that THC raised pulse with or without CBD, with no difference between the two; Nicholson et al. (2004; n=8) found no difference over 30 minutes; Karniol et al. (1974; n=40, 5 per group) described a further rise with oral CBD 15 mg and a smaller rise with 30 or 60 mg added to oral THC 30 mg. Three studies measured blood pressure: Guy and Robson (2003) reported mean systolic falls at 3 hours of 10.3 mmHg after THC 10 mg alone, 4.4 mmHg with CBD 10 mg and 5.1 mmHg after placebo; T. P. Freeman et al. (2018; n=17) found diastolic pressure raised after THC 8 mg alone but not with CBD 10 mg; Haney et al. (2016; n=31) found no differences after oral CBD 200, 400 or 800 mg before smoked THC (about 42 mg).
key_findings.locator: 3.6.2.1 Pulse rate, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 3.6.2.2 Blood pressure

key_findings.finding: Of nine studies of subjective intoxication, two reported that CBD reduced it: Dalton et al. (1976; n=15 in the text), smoked THC 0.025 mg/kg with smoked CBD 0.150 mg/kg, and Zuardi et al. (1982; n=8), oral THC 0.5 mg/kg with oral CBD 1 mg/kg (ARCI-Ma). Seven found no evidence that CBD changed intoxication. The discussion concludes that participants mostly experienced intoxication similarly with and without CBD.
key_findings.note: Dalton et al. (1976) appears on both sides in the text; Table 1 (pp. 66–67) shows two experiments: CBD smoked with THC reduced feeling high (16 enrolled, one withdrew), while oral CBD 30 minutes before smoked THC (8 men) altered no measure.

key_findings.finding: Three studies measured anxiety, two of them rated at some concerns or unclear risk. Karniol et al. (1974; parallel groups of 5): Grade 4 effects on the authors' 0–4 symptom scale (panic, an intense feeling of being watched, racing thoughts) in 4 of 5 participants after oral THC 30 mg alone, against 3 of 15 when oral CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg was added, and none at the highest CBD dose; no statistical test is reported in the review. Zuardi et al. (1982; crossover, n=8): oral CBD 1 mg/kg attenuated the STAI rise after oral THC 0.5 mg/kg. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): vaporised THC 13.75 mg with and without CBD 13.75 mg raised anxiety ratings and STAI at 15 minutes; only THC without CBD still raised them after an hour.

Three studies of psychotomimetic effects, none with risk-of-bias concerns. Bhattacharyya et al. (2010; pseudo-randomised crossover, n=6): intravenous THC 1.25 mg produced psychosis-like PANSS effects in 3 of 6, and intravenous CBD 5 mg beforehand prevented them (Table 1: in all three). Englund et al. (2013; parallel, n=48): after intravenous THC 1.5 mg, the mean PANSS increase did not differ between oral CBD 600 mg and placebo pre-treatment, but fewer people given CBD had a clinically significant rise in positive symptoms (at least 3 points) and paranoia (SSPS) was lower. Morgan et al. (2018; crossover, n=48): vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg did not differ in psychotomimetic effects; both raised BPRS negative symptoms and PSI scores, and the effects did not differ by frequency of cannabis use or trait schizotypy.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.5 Psychotomimetic and psychosis-like experiences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1, Bhattacharyya et al. (2010) row

key_findings.finding: THC alone impaired episodic memory in five studies. Englund et al. (2013; n=48): with oral CBD 600 mg beforehand, immediate recall after intravenous THC 1.5 mg was equally impaired but the delayed-recall impairment was lessened, and digit span was unchanged. Morgan et al. (2018; n=48): prose recall and N-back working memory were impaired equally after vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg. Karniol et al. (1974; n=40, 5 per group): the speeding of time production after oral THC 30 mg was absent with CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): DSST was impaired 20 minutes after THC 13.75 mg alone but not with CBD 13.75 mg, while divided attention was more impaired with CBD than after THC alone or placebo.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.6.1 Episodic memory; 3.6.6.2 Attention and working memory

key_findings.finding: Hindocha et al. (2015; n=48): vaporised THC 8 mg impaired recognition of facial emotions, and the impairment was absent when CBD 16 mg was added. Lawn et al. (2016; n=17): THC 8 mg increased sensitivity to the probability and size of rewards relative to both placebo and THC with CBD 10 mg; in the same study (T. P. Freeman et al., 2018) THC alone dampened brain responses to music, which did not differ from placebo when CBD was added.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.7 Emotion and reward processing, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Psychomotor performance and driving: Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): vaporised THC 13.75 mg with and without CBD 13.75 mg increased lane weaving in a simulated car-following task; Bird et al. (1980): oral CBD 0.320 mg/kg did not modify the impairment of standing steadiness and psychomotor coordination by oral THC 0.215 mg/kg; Dalton et al. (1976; n=16): smoked THC 0.025 mg/kg impaired standing steadiness, hand-eye coordination and dexterity with and without CBD 0.150 mg/kg; Roser et al. (2009; n=24): right-hand tapping was slower after oral THC 10 mg with CBD 5.4 mg but not after THC alone.

One sleep study (Nicholson et al., 2004; n=8; oromucosal THC 15 mg with or without CBD 15 mg). The text says THC with CBD increased wakefulness and stage 3 sleep and THC alone increased sleepiness 30 minutes after waking; Table 1 says THC with CBD, but not THC alone, decreased stage 3 sleep and increased time awake, and that both conditions increased sleepiness after waking.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.9 Sleep; Table 1, Nicholson et al. (2004) row
key_findings.note: The text and the table disagree on the direction of the stage 3 sleep finding and on sleepiness; the primary paper is needed before either is cited.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events visible in Table 1: in Arkell et al. (2019) one of 14 participants was discharged because of raised blood pressure and heart rate; in the Nadulski et al. (2005) sample three women had a panic attack (28 recruited, 20 to 24 analysed). The conditions in which these events happened are not stated.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Arkell et al. (2019) row (p. 65) and Nadulski et al. (2005) row (p. 70); Table 1 note d (p. 72)

key_findings.finding: The authors found no consistent pattern across routes, doses and THC:CBD ratios and could not determine a dose-response relation; they caution that oral CBD has low bioavailability (13–19%, cited from another source), so studies with low oral CBD doses (from 5.4 mg) should be read with caution. Conclusion: some evidence that CBD may reduce some effects of THC, with substantial variability between and within studies.

The discussion states that three studies showed significantly fewer participants with extreme anxiety and psychotic-like effects when CBD was added, and proposes that CBD may act only when THC's effects are extreme, since in Englund et al. (2013) CBD reduced clinically significant increases but not the mean increase.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the combined condition of Arkell et al. (2019) as vaporised THC 3.75 mg with CBD 13.75 mg (Intervention column, p. 65), while the text gives THC 13.75 mg with CBD 13.75 mg throughout (pp. 17, 22, 25, 26, 29). Table 1 also shows that the THC-alone condition contained up to 1.25 mg CBD.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table value looks like a typing error, but claims about this study's dose ratio or plasma THC finding should be checked against the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Nicholson et al. (2004) is described inconsistently: the pulse section gives sublingual drops of THC 10 mg with or without CBD 10 mg (p. 19), while the sleep section and Table 1 give oromucosal spray with 15 mg each (pp. 30, 71); the text says THC with CBD increased stage 3 sleep (p. 30) where Table 1 says it decreased it (p. 71); and Table 1 rates the study at low risk of bias although its design entry says randomisation was not indicated.
reporting_issues.consequence: No claim about CBD and sleep, or about this study's doses, can rest on the review; the direction of the sleep finding is unknown from this source.

reporting_issues.issue: The size of Bird et al. (1980) appears three ways: 161 recruited with six excluded in Table 1 (p. 66), which matches the stated maximum sample of 155 (p. 13) and the total of 466; 166 divided into 16 groups in Table 1 note a (p. 72); and n=116 in the text (p. 29).
reporting_issues.consequence: 155 is the figure consistent with the review's totals (editors' arithmetic); the others are errors.

reporting_issues.issue: The group sizes of Englund et al. (2013) are reversed between the body of Table 1 (26 placebo, 22 CBD; p. 67) and its note b (22 placebo, 26 CBD; p. 72); the text uses n=36 for the plasma comparison (p. 19) and n=48 elsewhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: Arm sizes for this trial must be taken from the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Dalton et al. (1976) contributed two experiments, counted as two studies in Table 1 (pp. 66–67) but named once in the text. This makes the text's counts look inconsistent (ten low-risk studies with nine named, p. 16) and places Dalton on both sides of the subjective-intoxication finding (p. 21). The sample is given as 15 (p. 21) and 16 (pp. 26, 29), and the CBD pre-treatment is described as smoked in the text (p. 15) but oral in Table 1 (p. 66).
reporting_issues.consequence: The study counts in the text are correct only if both experiments are counted; claims should name the experiment (CBD smoked with THC versus oral CBD before THC).

reporting_issues.issue: The summary of routes and doses (Treatment characteristics, p. 15) does not match Table 1: it counts two vaporised-THC studies at 8 mg and six oral, where Table 1 has three vaporised (including Arkell et al., 2019, at 13.75 mg) and five oral; its CBD route counts add to 15, not 16; its vaporised CBD range starts at 4 mg, a dose no study in Table 1 used (10, 13.75 and 16 mg); and its smoked CBD range reaches 0.320 mg/kg, which is the oral dose of Bird et al. (1980). Counts are the editors' from Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dose and route ranges for CBD and THC should be taken from Table 1, study by study, not from the summary paragraph.

reporting_issues.issue: Wall et al. (2019) is listed in two different study rows of Table 1, with the 48-person study (p. 68) and with the 17-person study (p. 70), while the text places it with the 17-person music-fMRI study (p. 28); Hindocha et al. (2019), the 48-person genetics analysis, is not named in Table 1, and the list of included articles under Study characteristics (p. 13) omits it and Wall et al. (2019) (editors' count: 21 of the 23 articles named).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which sample an article belongs to must be checked before treating findings as independent; the two UCL studies contribute six articles between them.

reporting_issues.issue: The risk-of-bias tool is named as RoB 2 but cited to Higgins et al. (2011) in the methods (p. 12) and to Higgins et al. (2016) in the limitations (p. 37); the anxiety section calls two studies unclear risk (p. 21) where Table 1 says some concerns; and Table 1 rates as low risk a study described as pseudo-randomised (Bhattacharyya et al., 2010; p. 65).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's low-risk ratings cannot be taken at face value for randomisation; the domain table (Appendix G) would be needed.

reporting_issues.issue: In the genetics paragraph, the sentence on FAAH carriers after THC with CBD reads that CC and A carriers did differ, introduced as a contrast to a difference after THC alone, which suggests a missing negation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of this genetic finding cannot be cited from the review.

N of the journal pre-proof'). This is not the version of record (Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 2019;107:696–712, not read), so pages differ from the published article. All text, the reference list and Table 1 (pp. 65–72) read; text pages checked on 100-dpi renderings, Table 1 on 150-dpi renderings and the Arkell et al. intervention cell at 300 dpi.
